extractions.value: Lorish et al. proposed diagnostic criteria for stiff-person syndrome including: Stiffness and rigidity in axial muscles; Progression of stiffness to include proximal limb muscles; Abnormal axial posture (lumbar hyperlordosis); Superimposed episodic spasms precipitated by sudden movement, emotional upsets and unexpected auditory and somaesthetic stimuli (startle phenomenon); Absence of brainstem, pyramidal, extrapyramidal, and lower motor neuron (LMN) signs, sphincter and sensory disturbance, and cognitive involvement; Electromyography findings consistent with continuous motor unit activity in at least one axial muscle that may be abolished with administration of diazepam. Positive amphiphysin antibody titer; Subsequent EMG testing was also consistent with stiff person syndrome

extractions.value: Initial misdiagnoses included psychogenic dystonia and presumed Lyme disease with co-infection with Babesia and Bartonella. The patient was treated with doxycycline, atovaquone, clarithromycin, nystatin, rifampin and hydroxychloroquine. Genetic testing was negative for pathogenic germline variants in ATM, BARD1, BRCA1, BRCA2, BRIP1, CDH1, CHEK2, NBN, NF1, PALB2, PTEN, RAD50, STK11 and TP53. Taxane-based chemotherapy was avoided due to concerns of potential peripheral neuropathy.
extractions.quote: it was documented that psychogenic dystonia was thought to be the most likely explanation; Evaluation by a rheumatologist resulted in a diagnosis of presumed Lyme disease; Genetic testing was negative for pathogenic germline variants in ATM, BARD1, BRCA1, BRCA2, BRIP1, CDH1, CHEK2, NBN, NF1, PALB2, PTEN, RAD50, STK11 and TP53; Taxane-based chemotherapy was avoided due to concerns of potential peripheral neuropathy further impairing the patient’s mobility
